claims.text: Degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is primarily controlled by the nature and evolution of its oxide scale.
Synergistic interactions between Al and Cr form an Al-enriched inner barrier and a Cr-rich outer oxide layer.
The proposed Al/Cr dual-layer scale initially protects the alloy in oxidizing environments.
Reducing conditions reverse diffusion gradients and thereby disrupt oxide-scale continuity.
Disruption of the scale under reducing conditions causes internal oxidation and accelerated degradation.
Exposure-driven degradation occurs without detrimental phase transformation of the bulk FCC matrix.
The as-fabricated alloy has a single-phase FCC microstructure with minimal pre-existing oxide coverage.
Preferential oxidation of Al and Cr produces a multilayer oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
Under oxidizing conditions, the oxide scale becomes continuous and adherent and retards oxygen ingress.
Under reducing conditions, altered diffusion gradients inhibit formation of a stable oxide and cause poor adhesion and localized internal oxidation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a thicker, denser, and more adherent dual-layer scale than reducing exposure.
The protective oxide formed under oxidizing exposure will produce a slower degradation rate.
Reducing exposure will produce a thinner, discontinuous, poorly adhered oxide scale with greater weight-change fluctuations and more internal oxidation.
Strength and fatigue performance will be maintained after oxidizing exposure.
Strength and fatigue performance will be compromised after reducing exposure because of subscale oxidation.
The predicted atmospheric contrast is most prominent at temperatures of at least 800 °C and exposure times of at least 10 hours.
At lower temperatures or shorter exposure times, oxidation-related degradation may be too subtle to distinguish between atmospheres.
Ti partitioning may influence oxide-scale formation and spallation kinetics.
Microstructural variations inherent to additive manufacturing may influence oxide-scale formation and spallation kinetics.
